analysis.one_liner: Creates an FDA pathway to approve lower-cost generic copies of biologic drugs.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a vote: introduced with bipartisan support in February 2007, it sat in the Senate health committee until the Congress ended in January 2009.
analysis.plain_summary: Biologic drugs — made from living cells to treat cancer, rheumatoid arthritis, diabetes, and other serious diseases — are among the most expensive medicines, and at the time there was no FDA process to approve cheaper copies of them. This bill would have created one: companies could file an abbreviated application showing their product is comparable to or interchangeable with the original, with an 8-month deadline for FDA action and limits on petitions and patent tactics used to stall approval. It was referred to the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee and never moved.
analysis.who_benefits: Patients who take biologic drugs, whose prices could fall as copycat products reach the market, and the generic and biosimilar manufacturers who would gain a legal pathway to sell those copies. Under the bill, the FDA would have to act on an application within 8 months and could not delay approval based on third-party petitions unless it finds a public-health reason [S2][S3].

how_it_helps.text: Establishes an abbreviated FDA approval process for 'comparable' and 'interchangeable' copies of already-approved biologic drugs, letting copies rely on the original product's safety data instead of repeating full clinical trials [S2][S3].

Requires the FDA to take final action on an application within 8 months of submission, and bars the agency from delaying approval because of petitions from outside parties unless it finds a delay is necessary to protect public health [S3].

Lets a copy be designated 'interchangeable' — expected to produce the same clinical result in any given patient — which is what allows a pharmacist to substitute it without a new prescription [S2][S3].

Sets up a structured patent process: brand manufacturers must disclose relevant patents within 60 days of a request and must sue within 45 days of notice or be limited to a reasonable royalty, reducing endless litigation as a delay tactic [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Brand-name biologic drug makers, whose long monopolies on expensive biologics would face copycat competition sooner, reducing the revenue that extended exclusivity protects. Taxpayers and insurers paying for these drugs would benefit rather than pay.

drawbacks.text: Biologics are large, complex molecules made in living cells, so copies can never be perfectly identical to the original; critics argue that approving them through an abbreviated pathway, especially with automatic substitution of 'interchangeable' products, carries more safety uncertainty than copying a simple chemical pill [S3].

The bill gives the first 'interchangeable' copy a period of market exclusivity — 180 days of marketing, or longer if the applicant is sued on patents — which delays the arrival of a second competitor and the deepest price cuts [S2][S3].

The patent-disclosure and 45-day lawsuit window creates a new litigation framework whose costs and disputes would fall on both brand and generic companies, with some of that expense ultimately reflected in drug prices [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit is large: biologic drugs routinely cost tens of thousands of dollars a year, and a functioning copy pathway is the main mechanism Congress eventually used to bring those prices down. The safety objections are real but were addressed by requiring clinical comparability data and an interchangeability standard. The bill's exclusivity and patent provisions tilt toward first movers rather than maximum competition, but on balance it would have shifted value from brand-drug monopolies to patients. Badly designed? No — though the version that finally became law in 2010 gave brand makers far longer exclusivity, showing how contested the design was.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced with bipartisan support and referred to the Senate health committee, which never took it up, and it died there when the Congress ended in January 2009.

narrative.text: Sen. Charles Schumer introduced the bill on February 15, 2007, joined by Sens. Clinton, Vitter, Collins, Leahy, and Stabenow as original cosponsors [S3][S5].
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee the same day [S5].

The only subsequent action in the entire 110th Congress was a 'star print' — a technical reordering of the printed bill — on February 27, 2007; the committee never held a markup or sent the bill to the floor [S5].
The Congress ended on January 3, 2009, with no vote ever held in either chamber [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Brand-name biologic drug makers, who kept their exclusive control of the market for expensive biologics for another three years until a version of this pathway was enacted in the 2010 health law — with a longer brand exclusivity period than this bill proposed.

for.name: Sen. Charles Schumer
for.role: Senator from New York; bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Access to Life-Saving Medicine Act and delivered introductory remarks on the floor.

for.name: Sens. Clinton, Vitter, Collins, Leahy, and Stabenow
for.role: Original cosponsors from New York, Louisiana, Maine, Vermont, and Michigan
for.what_they_did: Joined as original cosponsors at introduction, giving the bill bipartisan sponsorship across five states.

for.name: 3 of 7 cosponsors
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill (3 of the 7 cosponsors were Republicans).

against.name: HELP Committee leadership
against.role: Chair of the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee (Edward Kennedy, D-MA)
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a markup or a floor vote on the bill during the 110th Congress.

against.name: Brand-name biotech and pharmaceutical industry
against.what_they_did: Fought follow-on biologic legislation, pushing instead for long periods of market exclusivity before copies could be approved.

sides.party_line_note: Sponsorship was bipartisan — 7 cosponsors split 4 Democrats and 3 Republicans, including Republican Sens. Vitter and Collins as original cosponsors — and the bill's death was not a party-line vote but a committee that never acted [S4][S5].

industries.note: The bill would have ended their sole pathway to market for biologics by letting copy products rely on the original's safety data, cutting short the monopoly pricing on drugs that cost patients and insurers thousands of dollars a year. Their interest in blocking the pathway ran directly against patients' interest in cheaper medicine.

The bill creates the entire legal market they would sell into, complete with an interchangeability designation and 180 days of exclusivity for the first interchangeable copy. Their gain comes from lowering the price patients pay.

industries.industry: Pharmacy benefit managers and health insurers
industries.note: A cheaper substitute for expensive biologics reduces what insurers and plans pay, which flows back to premiums. The bill's interchangeability pathway is what makes substitution practical.
